transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. Homeland Security Secretary Mark Wayne
Mullen and other top intelligence officials testified on Capitol Hill today. They were
scheduled to talk about worldwide threats since the 9/11 attacks, but as NPR's Kat
Lahnstorff reports, the focus quickly shifted to more recent troubles.
The senior administration officials were questioned about a string of tech outages, most notably
the rare nationwide ground stop that stranded thousands of airline passengers Friday afternoon
and into the weekend. That closely coincided with outages of Microsoft Outlook, major banks,
and other services. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said that he understood that such
notable outages happening at the same time is raising questions from the American public,
but reiterated that they are all separate incidents associated with technical problems.
They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.
The Trump administration has been adamant that the outages are isolated and unconnected.
Kat Lahnstorff, NPR News, Washington.
Outgoing Louisiana Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, who chairs the Senate Health Committee,
said they would not consider the White House's pick to lead the National Science Foundation,
Jim O'Neill. Cassidy said O'Neill did not do enough to stand up for science during his
time as acting director for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Metta developed a plan to increase teenage Instagram use by building connections with schools across
the country, according to internal documents. But experts say the plan also makes teens
less safe online, as NPR's Katie McHugh reports.
Metta called the plan Project Gryffindor. It encourages students to add school banners
to their profiles and use directories to connect with other classmates.
Metta launched the school partnership program in 2025. Nearly 17,000 schools have signed
up. Publicly, Metta said the program is designed to improve student safety, help schools report
bullying and keep families informed about school activities.
Yet, cybersecurity experts say the program increases teens' vulnerability to scammers
and hackers, who often try to access their connections for blackmail and sex torsion
schemes. And experts say the program's student directories will make this easier to do.
Metta disputes his criticisms, saying the program provides meaningful safety protections.
Katie McHugh, NPR News, New York.
It was a mixed day on Wall Street, and NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow tumbled more
than 1 percent, while the tech-heavy NASDAQ rose.
Blue chip stocks suffered, with the Dow slumping more than 560 points. Nvidia shares also failed,
despite a better-than-expected earnings report from the computer chip giant on Tuesday. A
report from the Commerce Department on home-building activity shows a drop in permits last month
for future construction.
High mortgage rates have been a drag on the housing market. The Federal Reserve held short-term
interest rates steady last month, but newly released minutes from that meeting show most
Fed policymakers expect further rate hikes will be necessary to bring inflation under
control.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is visiting Venezuela and says the nations have signed
a deal to reestablish military ties, from training to intelligence sharing. The visit
underscores efforts by the Trump administration to deepen its influence in the country. Since
the U.S. ousted then-president Nicolas Maduro in January, interim president Delsi Rodriguez
says the agreements will allow the U.S. to offer training to Venezuela's armed forces.
The White House is celebrating historic improvements in drug overdose deaths, but Trump officials
also made misleading claims about who deserves credit for the progress, and PR's Brian Mann
reports.
In a statement, White House Office of National Drug Control Policy Director Sarah Carter
said fatal street drug overdoses are now at their lowest level in nearly a decade. She
suggested the gains have happened over the last 18 months under Trump. In fact, preliminary
data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows the biggest drop in
drug deaths happened in 2023 and 2024 when Biden was still in office. NPR asked the White
House about their misleading timeline. In an email to NPR, Carter said Biden deserves
no credit for his administration's fentanyl response. She blamed Biden for the spike in
drug deaths that occurred during the COVID pandemic. Brian Mann, NPR News.
Coyotes are already making their way across a new wildlife crossing set to officially
open next month over a Los Angeles-area freeway. The bridge has a landscape that's indistinguishable
from surrounding hillsides. It stretches 1,250 feet over U.S. 101 to give wildlife hemmed
in by urban sprawl a safe path to the nearby Santa Monica Mountains and beyond.
I'm Rylan Barton. This is NPR News.

topics.text: Homeland Security Secretary Mullen and intelligence officials testify on Capitol Hill, tech outages dominate questioning
Senator Bill Cassidy says Health Committee won't consider Jim O'Neill's nomination to lead National Science Foundation
Meta's Project Gryffindor school partnership program on Instagram criticized as making teens less safe online
Dow drops over 1 percent while Nasdaq rises; Nvidia shares fall despite strong earnings, housing permits decline
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visits Venezuela, signs deal to reestablish military ties with interim president Rodriguez
White House claims credit for drop in overdose deaths, but data shows the biggest declines came under Biden
Coyotes already using new wildlife crossing spanning U.S. 101 in Los Angeles area, opening next month
